newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-strong UK money M4 data point to rates rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-strong UK money M4 data point to rates rise.

text.p: British broad money supply grew strongly in May, providing further evidence that consumer spending is powering ahead and increasing the likelihood that interest rates, and possibly taxes, will rise soon.

The Bank of England said M4 money supply rose a seasonally adjusted 1.3 percent in May, taking the year-on-year growth rate to a robust 11.1 percent from 10.2 percent in April. This was well above the official three to nine percent monitoring range.
M4 is a broad measure which comprises notes and coins in circulation, personal and commercial bank deposits and certificates of deposit.

Economists said the figures would refuel the Bank of England's anxiety about inflationary pressures and made it more likely that official interest rates, raised twice in the last two months to their present 6.5 percent, would go even higher.

"I think we should see a half-point increase in base rates at the next meeting and I don't think that can be the end of the tightening in monetary policy this year," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse.
The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee, empowered by the Labour government to set interest rates, holds its next meeting on July 10, a week after Labour's first budget on July 2.

The Bank is particularly worried about the impact on consumer spending of "windfalls" totalling an estimated 30 billion pounds which millions of Britons will receive as mutually owned building societies turn themselves into banks.

Some economists said that if Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown wants to stave off further interest rate rises, he would need to increases taxes by more than the two to three billion pounds financial markets are expecting.
"It's got to be at least five billion pounds," said HSBC UK economist Jonathan Loynes. "I don't think anything less is going to keep the Bank at bay."

If Brown delivers a tight budget, with tax rises carefully targeted at the consumer, then he might be able to restrict further rate rises this year to another quarter point, or even prevent them going up at all, Loynes said.
"If he doesn't, you're looking at another 1/2 point on rates by the end of the year."

However, Brown limited his room for manoeuvre before the May 1 election by promising not to increase income tax rates and to live within tight public spending limits set by the former Conservative government.

James Barty, chief UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said M4 joined recent industrial production and retail sales data in pointing to buoyant economic activity to which the authorities would have to respond.
"With the Chancellor constrained by political commitments not to raise personal taxes, the Bank of England will have to push interest rates higher instead," he said.

Separate figures from the British Bankers' Association showed total sterling lending by major British banks to the personal sector rose a seasonally adjusted 3.53 billion pounds in May and consumer credit was particularly strong.
"Once again the strength of lending to persons was the outstanding feature in the major banks' figures for May," its director-general Tim Sweeney said.

"Whilst mortgage lending remained buoyant, it was the rise in consumer credit of approaching 600 million that is particularly eye-catching. This was around double the figure a year earlier and some 40 percent above the recent monthly average."
